
Most amateur teams still keep score on paper. After the season, the
scorebook holds everything a coach needs to know: who gets on base, who puts
the ball in play, and how hard each pitcher has been worked. But it takes an
evening with a calculator to get any of it out. This vignette follows a coach
through four questions, using the scorecards the dAImond Inning app has
already read.

```{r setup}
library(daimondstats)
```

## Use case 1: load and explore the season

The package ships `reviewed_scorecards`, 179 plate appearances from five real
scorecards. Each row is one plate appearance, already reviewed against the
official record, so `needs_review` is `FALSE` everywhere.

```{r explore}
dim(reviewed_scorecards)
table(reviewed_scorecards$team)
sort(table(reviewed_scorecards$play), decreasing = TRUE)
```

Your own games come in one of two ways. A single game's CSV export from the
app goes through `import_scorecards()`:

```{r import}
path <- system.file("extdata", "demo_plays.csv", package = "daimondstats")
one_game <- import_scorecards(path, game_id = "demo-01")
head(one_game, 3)
```

For a whole season, connect to your account with an API key (Settings, API
keys in the app) and download everything at once. This needs the internet
and a key, so it is not run here:

```{r api, eval = FALSE}
daimond_auth("di_pat_...")          # once per R session
season <- daimond_games(from = "2026-04-01", to = "2026-07-31")
plays <- season$plays[!season$plays$needs_review, ]
```

Either way, the result has the same columns, so every function below works
on it.

## Use case 2: who actually gets on base?

In youth baseball the defense makes a lot of errors. Batting average and OBP
treat reaching on an error as an out, which hides batters who put the ball in
play and force the defense to make a play. `calculate_youth_stats()` adds
**OBPE**, on-base percentage that counts reaching on an error, alongside
isolated power (ISO), strikeout and walk rates, and BABIP.

```{r youth}
youth <- calculate_youth_stats(reviewed_scorecards, min_pa = 4)
cols <- c("team", "player", "PA", "ROE", "OBP", "OBPE", "ISO", "K_rate")
head(youth[order(-youth$OBPE), cols], 8)
```

These are major league games, so errors are rare and OBPE barely moves. In
youth games the gap between OBP and OBPE is often several points. Two things
to keep in mind:

* Every one of these players has only one game here. `small_sample` marks
  anyone under `min_pa` plate appearances (25 by default). A handful of games
  can swing any rate a long way.
* Pooling uses the exact team and player name. Spell a player's name the same
  way on every scorecard, or correct it in the app first.

Use `by = "game"` to see a player's game-by-game line instead of the season.

## Use case 3: check pitch counts against Pitch Smart

Most leagues follow the MLB/USA Baseball Pitch Smart guidelines: a daily
maximum by age, and required days of rest that depend on how many pitches were
thrown. `demo_pitch_log` is a fictional month for a 12U staff.

```{r pitch-log}
demo_pitch_log
checks <- check_pitch_counts(demo_pitch_log)
checks[checks$status != "ok",
       c("pitcher", "date", "pitches", "daily_max", "next_eligible", "status")]
```

Two problems show up. Mia Torres threw 66 pitches on May 2, which requires
four days of rest, but she pitched again on May 6, a day early. Leo Park, who
is 11, threw 88 pitches on May 23, three over his age group's limit of 85.
Note that Mia's two doubleheader appearances on May 9 were added together,
because the limit applies to the whole day.

The `next_eligible` column answers the question a coach has before every
game: who can pitch today?

```{r eligible}
game_day <- as.Date("2026-05-24")
latest <- tapply(checks$next_eligible, checks$pitcher, max)
data.frame(pitcher = names(latest),
           available = as.Date(latest, origin = "1970-01-01") <= game_day)
```

If your league is stricter, pass an edited copy of `pitch_smart_rules`:

```{r strict}
strict <- pitch_smart_rules
strict$daily_max[strict$age_min == 11] <- 75L
check_pitch_counts(demo_pitch_log, rules = strict)$status
```

## Use case 4: share a one-page season report

`season_report()` puts the batting table, an on-base chart, and the
pitch-count flags into one HTML file that opens in any browser and prints
on a single page. Parents and players can read it without R.

```{r report}
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "season-report.html")
season_report(reviewed_scorecards, out, title = "Five scored games",
              pitch_check = checks, min_pa = 4, overwrite = TRUE)
file.exists(out)
```

To see the chart from the report here, compare OBP with OBPE directly:

```{r obpe-plot, fig.alt = "Bar chart comparing OBP and OBPE for the batters with the most plate appearances"}
top <- head(youth[order(-youth$PA, -youth$OBPE), ], 10)
barplot(rbind(top$OBP, top$OBPE - top$OBP), names.arg = top$player,
        horiz = TRUE, las = 1, col = c("#0875D1", "#9CC9F0"), border = NA,
        xlim = c(0, 1), cex.names = 0.7,
        xlab = "On base (dark) plus reached on error (light)")
```

## What the package does not do

* It does not read images. The dAImond Inning app reads the scorecard; this
  package analyzes what was read and reviewed.
* It refuses rows still marked for review instead of guessing.
* Quality at-bats need pitch-by-pitch counts, which scorecard cells do not
  record, so they are left out.
* Pitch counts come from the scorecard's pitcher box. Pitching for another
  team or league is invisible to the check.

For run value (RE24) and comparing the games you scored with a team's full
season, see `vignette("from-scorecard-to-run-value")`.
